body.heading: Same atoms, different architecture
paragraphs: Diamond and graphite could hardly behave more differently — one is the hardest natural material, the other is soft enough to leave a mark on paper — yet both are pure carbon, nothing else. Forms of the same element with different structures are called allotropes, and carbon is the great show-off of the family: the difference is entirely in how its atoms are connected.

In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four neighbours in a rigid three-dimensional pyramid pattern that extends through the whole crystal. There are no weak directions; to scratch a diamond you must break strong bonds, and almost nothing can.

body.heading: Layers that slide
paragraphs: Graphite arranges the same atoms into flat sheets. Within each sheet the atoms are strongly bonded in hexagons, but between the sheets there are only weak attractions — plus a sea of loose electrons that lets graphite conduct electricity, which diamond cannot do. Press a pencil to paper and the sheets shear off in flakes: that grey line is graphite layers, sacrificed by the thousand.

Heat graphite to extreme temperatures and pressures and it will reorganise into diamond; leave a diamond for geological ages and it very slowly tends the other way — graphite is carbon's most stable form, and every diamond is, in the strictest sense, temporary. Nature makes diamonds deep in the Earth and brings them up in volcanic eruptions; factories now grow them in presses and vapour chambers.

body.heading: Newer forms of an old element
paragraphs: The family keeps growing. In 1985 scientists found carbon atoms arranged as hollow footballs of sixty atoms — fullerenes, nicknamed buckyballs. In 2004, researchers isolated graphene: a single sheet of graphite's hexagons, one atom thick, transparent, flexible, and sheet-for-sheet stronger than steel.

Soot, the black residue of a smoky flame, is carbon too — mostly disordered, with no grand pattern at all. One element, endlessly rearranged: gem, pencil, powder and the most studied material of the century.

description: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Only the arrangement of their atoms differs — and that changes everything about them.
